message:
fix(update): the host was still waiting on its UI thread, and sign-out was not an owner change

Three defects, and the first one is what happens when a fix is applied to
one of two places and reported as applied to both. The client's credential
wait was moved to a thread; the host's was not. Its Serve sat before the
thread that follows it, so clicking the menu item blocked the window for up
to two minutes.

The second was a data race rather than a stale read. The owner predicate ran
on a background thread and read the account, machine id, server address,
token and epoch straight out of shared state while the UI thread's sign-in
and sign-out wrote them. A std::string is not something to read while
another thread assigns it. There is a mutex now and a single
current_update_endpoint() that takes one snapshot under it -- read
separately, those five values can straddle a sign-out and describe an owner
that never existed at any one moment.

The third: sign_out cleared the token and left the epoch alone, so with
keepAccount the account and machine id were unchanged and same_owner_as
stayed true. The final check also had no condition that a credential still
exists, so an empty token passed it. Signing out therefore did not stop an
attempt already in flight from being acknowledged. Sign-out bumps the epoch
now on both sides, and the final condition requires a credential -- two
guards because either one alone is a single point of failure for the same
outcome.

The regression no longer uses a stub predicate. It builds two endpoints with
the product's own builder -- one as held at launch, one as held after
sign_out -- and compares them with the product's own comparison. A stub
proves the wiring and says nothing about whether a real sign-out reads as a
different owner. Alongside it: a re-login, which has a perfectly good token
and an identical url, and an unchanged owner that is acknowledged, without
which every refusal above would also pass for a build that acknowledges
nothing.
